chapter_title: Design of Micropiles for Structure Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: A typical structural micropile has an upper length with permanent casing and a center bar, and a lower grouted bond length with the bar (Figure 5-1). Geotechnical capacity is sensitive to drilling, flushing and grouting, so load testing to verify the assumed grout-ground shaft resistance is part of the design. Unlike drilled shafts, micropile design is usually controlled by structural considerations. Table 5-1 lists the 12 design steps and other considerations; Sample Problem No. 1 is a complete design.
sections.body: (pp. 5-1 to 5-3) A typical micropile cross section for structural foundation support (Figure 5-1) has an upper length reinforced with a permanent steel casing and a center reinforcing bar, and a lower grouted bond length reinforced with the center bar. The geotechnical capacity is sensitive to the construction process, especially drilling, flushing the cuttings and grouting, so verifying by load testing the shaft resistance at the grout-ground interface assumed in design is essential to confirm structure safety, and load testing should be considered part of the design. The basic philosophy differs little from that for a drilled shaft: the system must sustain the anticipated loads with components at safe stress levels and displacements within tolerable limits. Drilled shafts, with large cross sections and high structural capacity and stiffness, are normally governed by geotechnical capacity (side and base resistance); micropiles, with small cross sections, are usually controlled by structural considerations, and the high grout-to-ground capacities from pressure grouting typically give high geotechnical capacities. This chapter presents a step-by-step generalized design method for structural foundations, outlined in Table 5-1, with a complete design in Sample Problem No. 1. Table 5-1 steps: (1) identify project requirements and evaluate feasibility; (2) review available information and perform subsurface exploration and laboratory testing; (3) develop all loading combinations; (4) preliminary design (spacing, length, cross section); (5) allowable structural capacity of the cased length; (6) of the uncased length; (7) compare design loads with Steps 5 and 6 and modify the section if necessary; (8) geotechnical capacity (bond stratum, bond stress and length, group compression and uplift capacity); (9) group settlement; (10) micropile to footing connection; (11) load testing program; (12) drawings and specifications. Other design considerations: corrosion protection (a critical component of all designs), plunge length, end bearing micropiles, downdrag, lateral loads on single vertical micropiles and on groups, buckling, seismic.

sections.title: Step 1: Evaluate Project Requirements and Micropile Feasibility
sections.summary: Compare foundation types (spread footings or mats, with or without ground improvement; driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles) by superstructure needs, ground and cost; spread footings are generally cheaper and deep foundations should not be used indiscriminately (FHWA NHI-05-042). Micropiles are usually costlier than driven piles or shafts, so they suit boulders or debris, difficult access or low overhead, voids (karst, mines), vibration limits, or underpinning needing strict vibration or settlement control. Micropiles in rock have been tested to 4,500 kN (1,000 kips).
sections.body: (pp. 5-3 to 5-5) Various foundation types should be considered systematically and the optimum selected from superstructure requirements, subsurface conditions and cost: shallow foundations (spread footings or mats, with or without ground improvement) or deep foundations (driven piles, drilled shafts or micropiles). Spread footings are generally more economical than deep foundations and should be considered, including with ground improvement; deep foundations should not be used indiscriminately for all subsurface conditions and structures. Feasibility evaluations for shallow foundations, driven piles and drilled shafts are in FHWA NHI-05-042 (2005). Where deep foundations are judged most appropriate, micropiles should be compared with driven piles and drilled shafts; where driven piles or shafts are feasible but costly because of ground or other constraints, micropile cost effectiveness should be investigated, and bidding alternative systems may give the most cost-effective option. In many cases driven piles or drilled shafts will be more cost-effective, so micropiles are limited to projects with technical constraints that make those difficult to impossible. Micropiles may be cost-effective where: subsurface conditions make driven piles or shafts difficult and expensive (significant boulders, cobbles or large debris); access is difficult or overhead clearance limited (inside existing structures, under bridge decks); subsurface voids may exist (collapsible ground, karst, underground mines); vibration limits preclude conventional equipment; or underpinning or retrofitting needs strict control of vibrations or settlements. Micropile capacities continue to increase with experience; micropiles in rock have been tested to ultimate loads as high as 4,500 kN (1,000 kips), and for high capacity micropiles the cost per unit capacity may be comparable to driven piles. Project costs are evaluated in Chapter 10; for driven pile cost per unit capacity see FHWA NHI-05-042 (2005).

sections.title: Step 2: Review Available Information and Geotechnical Data
sections.summary: Exploration and testing are as for driven piles (FHWA NHI-05-042) or drilled shafts (FHWA-HI-99-025); see AASHTO (1988), FHWA NHI-01-031 and GEC 5. Minimum information: geology, site history, boring logs with SPT or CPT and groundwater, rock logs with RQD, index tests, a soil profile, strength and compressibility, corrosive or contaminated conditions, liquefiable, expansive or void-prone ground. Table 5-2 gives minimum borings; karst may need a boring at each micropile; battered piles need borings at the offset bond zone.
sections.body: (pp. 5-5 to 5-7) Subsurface exploration, laboratory testing and evaluation of design parameters for structural micropiles are similar to those for driven piles (FHWA NHI-05-042, 2005) or drilled shafts (FHWA-HI-99-025, 1999). The program should be preceded by a review of published and unpublished information at and near the site, a visual site inspection and design of the exploration program; guidance is in the AASHTO Manual on Subsurface Investigations (1988), FHWA NHI-01-031 (2001) and GEC 5, Evaluation of Soil and Rock Properties (2002). At a minimum, information to analyze foundation stability and settlement includes: regional and local geology; site history (mining, previous excavations, construction problems, adjacent utilities, basements or foundations, possible contaminated materials); boring logs with soil descriptions and classification, unit weights, moisture contents, SPT or CPT values and groundwater; for rock, classifications, penetration rates, weathering and fracturing, recovery and RQD, and driller's observations; Atterberg limits (silty or clayey soils) and grain size analyses; a subsurface profile along the structure showing soil type, groundwater and SPT values; estimated soil and/or rock shear strength and compressibility; hazardous, contaminated or corrosive conditions (indicators: low resistivity, lead, sulfates, chlorides, corrosion of existing features); and project-specific conditions such as liquefiable layers, expansive or dispersive soils, and voids from solution weathering or mining. Table 5-2 gives minimum boring spacing and depth as a first step only; heterogeneous soil or rock will likely need more. In karst it may be necessary to bore at each micropile location. For battered micropiles the bond length is offset from the footing, and borings should be located to obtain information on the bond zone soils. All geotechnical data interpretations should be provided, and the strata can be verified during installation by logging penetration rates, drilling action, flush return and cuttings.

sections.title: Step 3: Develop Applicable Loading Combinations
sections.summary: State DOT projects use AASHTO Standard Specifications (ASD or LFD) or AASHTO LRFD for loads and combinations; the structural engineer usually supplies maximum compression, tension and overturning moments, with lateral, seismic and downdrag cases. For most applications the cap may be taken as rigid and the rigid cap method used to distribute overturning to micropiles; large groups, thin caps, wide spacing, or micropiles with pre-existing elements of different stiffness may need soil-structure interaction analysis (Section 5.19.3).
sections.body: (p. 5-7) For state DOT projects, loadings, load combinations and terminology typically come from the AASHTO Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges (allowable stress design (ASD) or load factor design (LFD)) or the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications. Under any approach, individual loads are combined into a series of load combinations to be checked. The required loads (e.g., maximum compression, maximum tension, maximum transverse and longitudinal overturning moments) are usually provided by the structural engineer in a design criteria package; other cases may include lateral loads, seismic loads and downdrag. For most applications it is sufficiently accurate to assume the cap is perfectly rigid (free to rotate about all axes but not bending), so the rigid cap method can distribute axial forces from overturning moments to individual elements. For large pile groups, relatively thin caps and/or widely spaced elements a more sophisticated soil-structure interaction analysis may be required, and since micropiles are often used with pre-existing foundation elements, differences in stiffness may also require such analyses (Section 5.19.3).
key_points: Loads and combinations from AASHTO Standard Specifications (ASD or LFD) or AASHTO LRFD

sections.title: Selection of Micropile Spacing
sections.summary: Center-to-center spacing should be at least 760 mm (30 in.) or 3 diameters, whichever is greater (a driven pile criterion allowing for drilling deviation and reducing group effects). Retrofit spacing depends on the existing footing's condition, access and loads; for small loads (e.g., under 450 kN (100 kips)) micropiles may be drilled through the footing, while larger loads or deteriorated footings may need a new footing doweled to the old. The Owner may set the layout or let the Contractor choose fewer higher-capacity micropiles.
sections.body: (p. 5-8) In all cases the center-to-center spacing between micropiles should be at least 760 mm (30 in.) or 3 micropile diameters, whichever is greater; this criterion, originally developed for driven piles, allows for drilling deviations over significant depths and reduces group effects between adjacent micropiles. Spacing also depends on the application: for retrofit of an existing footing it depends on the footing's condition, access to it and the loads to be resisted. Where relatively small design loads are involved (e.g., less than 450 kN (100 kips)) it may be feasible to drill micropiles through the existing foundation and still develop sufficient load transfer; where larger loads are required or the foundation has deteriorated, a new footing may be built around the existing one and positively connected with steel dowels or other devices. Spacing and layout may be selected by the Owner in the Plans, or the Specifications may let the Contractor select the number and layout, giving flexibility to use fewer higher capacity micropiles instead of a baseline with more lower capacity micropiles.

sections.title: Selection of Micropile Length
sections.summary: Length is set by the bond length needed in a suitable stratum (Section 5.9), plus penetration to resist downdrag and uplift and to add lateral resistance where scour or other lateral loads matter. Track rigs can exceed 90 m (300 ft), but a practical limit for most projects is on the order of 30 m (100 ft).
sections.body: (pp. 5-8 to 5-9) The total length of a micropile is selected so the required geotechnical capacity is developed by skin friction (side resistance) between grout and ground over a suitable length in an appropriate stratum (Section 5.9). Length is also controlled by penetration needed to resist downdrag and uplift and to provide additional lateral resistance where scour or other lateral loads must be considered. Common track-drilling equipment can achieve lengths greater than 90 m (300 ft), but such lengths would be very expensive, and a practical limit for most projects may be on the order of 30 m (100 ft).
key_points: Length set by the bond length in a suitable stratum (Section 5.9)

sections.title: Selection of Micropile Cross Section
sections.summary: Up to one half of the section may be steel casing and/or bars. Common U.S. casings are 141 mm (5-1/2 in.), 178 mm (7 in.) and 245 mm (9-5/8 in.) OD at 552 MPa (80 ksi), 178 mm most common (Tables 4-2 to 4-5). Fewer higher capacity micropiles are preferable; casing resists lateral load and high axial load better (178 mm casing has about 2.5 times the steel of a 2.25-in. bar), so above about 900 kN (200 kips) allowable casing is likely needed. Grout-to-steel bond (1.0-1.75 MPa smooth, 2.0-3.5 MPa deformed) rarely governs.
sections.body: (p. 5-9) To carry required axial loads it is not uncommon for up to one half of the micropile cross section to be steel casing and/or reinforcing bar(s). Common casing sizes are preferred to avoid material delays; the most common U.S. sizes are 141 mm (5-1/2 in.), 178 mm (7 in.) and 245 mm (9-5/8 in.) outside diameter with a nominal yield stress of 552 MPa (80 ksi), the 178 mm casing being the most common; Tables 4-2 to 4-5 give reinforcement properties. It is generally preferable to install fewer higher capacity micropiles than more lower capacity ones, requiring less total drilling and reducing cost. Steel casing is more efficient than bars alone for resisting lateral loads, limiting lateral deflection and achieving high axial capacity: a 178 mm (7-in.) casing has about 2.5 times the steel area of a 2.25-in. diameter bar, so for allowable axial loads greater than approximately 900 kN (200 kips) casing would likely be required. Grout-to-bar bond allows composite action and transfers load from steel to ground; typical ultimate bond values are 1.0 to 1.75 MPa (145 to 254 psi) for smooth bars and pipe and 2.0 to 3.5 MPa (290 to 508 psi) for deformed bars (ACI 318). Flaky rust lowers bond, but wiping off the loosest rust leaves a rougher surface with bond equal to or greater than unrusted bar; loose powdery rust after short exposure has no significant effect. In the majority of cases grout-to-steel bond does not govern; the allowable load is generally controlled by the structural strength of the section (Steps 5 and 6).

Ultimate grout-to-steel bond: 1.0-1.75 MPa (145-254 psi) smooth bars and pipe; 2.0-3.5 MPa (290-508 psi) deformed bars (ACI 318)

sections.title: Selection of Micropile Type
sections.summary: Selection of micropile type (A, B, C, D; Chapter 4) should be left to the Contractor, who should state proposed drilling and grouting methods in the bid. The Owner may disallow techniques from experience (e.g., methods that increase caving in sandy ground where surface movement must be limited) and should give performance criteria such as structure movements.
sections.body: (p. 5-10) Micropile types A, B, C and D are described in Chapter 4. Selection of the type should be left to the Contractor, but the Owner should require the Contractor to provide its proposed drilling and grouting methods in the bid. From previous experience the Owner may disallow certain drilling techniques for project constraints; e.g., limiting surface ground movements in sandy ground may preclude techniques known to increase caving. The Owner should provide specific performance criteria (e.g., movements of structures) in the bid package so the Contractor can select an appropriate industry-accepted drilling and grouting procedure.

Owner requires the proposed drilling and grouting methods with the bid

sections.title: Step 5: Structural Design of Micropile Cased Length
sections.summary: Pc-allowable = 0.4 f'c-grout Agrout + 0.47 Fy-steel (Abar + Acasing) (Eq. 5-1), Fy-steel the least of casing yield, bar yield and 600 MPa (87 ksi) (grout strain 0.003 x 200,000 MPa); Pt-allowable = 0.55 Fy-steel (Abar + Acasing) (Eq. 5-2). Reduce casing OD for corrosion; in aggressive ground take Acasing = 0 in tension; joint data if tension exceeds 25 percent of intact casing capacity. Combined stress per AASHTO 10.36 (Eqs. 5-3 to 5-5, FS 2.12, K = 1.0) or Richards and Rothbauer (Eq. 5-6).
sections.body: (pp. 5-10 to 5-17) 1) Allowable compression load for the cased length: Pc-allowable = [0.4 f'c-grout x Agrout + 0.47 Fy-steel (Abar + Acasing)] (Eq. 5-1), where f'c is the grout unconfined compressive strength (typically 28-day), Agrout the grout area inside the casing only (discount grout outside the casing), Fy-steel the steel yield stress, Abar the bar area (if used) and Acasing the casing area. Strain compatibility: allowable compressive stresses are limited to the minimum for any component, so Fy-steel in Eq. 5-1 is the minimum of (1) casing yield stress, (2) bar yield stress and (3) the maximum stress based on grout failure; AASHTO (2002) 8.16.2.3 limits the usable concrete strain to 0.003, so steel is limited to E x 0.003 = 200,000 MPa x 0.003 = 600 MPa (87 ksi). E.g., casing 241 MPa (36 ksi), bar 520 MPa (75 ksi), grout limit 600 MPa: use 241 MPa (36 ksi). Example (Figure 5-2: 5-1/2 in. OD x 0.415 in. N80 casing, 4,000 psi grout): ID = 4.67 in., Acasing = 6.63 in.2, Agrout = (pi/4)(5.5 in.)^2 - 6.63 = 17.13 in.2, Fy = min(80, 87) = 80 ksi, Pc-allowable = 0.4(4 ksi)(17.13) + 0.47(80 ksi)(6.63) = 276 kips. Coupled sections: casing sections may be 1 m or shorter in very low overhead (the print refers to Chapter 3); bar couplers typically provide at least 125 percent of the bar yield strength, so intact bar properties can be used; a properly designed threaded casing joint filled with grout can give compressive capacity about equal to the intact casing (the grout keeps the male half from deforming inward); coupled strength is confirmed by proof and verification testing. Corrosion: the casing outside diameter is reduced for corrosion losses over the design life depending on ground aggressivity (Section 5.14); the bar area is not reduced for compression, coatings and grout cover protecting it. Buckling of cased length of micropile: in very weak ground or karst the allowable compression may need reduction for buckling (Section 5.20). 2) Allowable tension load: Pt-allowable = 0.55 Fy-steel x (Abar + Acasing) (Eq. 5-2), Fy-steel the minimum yield of bar and casing. In aggressive ground (Section 5.14) the casing may conservatively be assumed ineffective in tension (Acasing = 0) and the bar designed for the entire tension load. Tension affects threaded joint integrity more because of the reduced wall thickness; no testing standard exists, so if tension above 25 percent of the allowable tension on intact casing is to be resisted by flush-joint threaded casing, the Owner should require the contractor to demonstrate the joint, reviewed by a qualified engineer. 3) Combined axial compression and bending: lateral loads or moments at the ground surface add bending stresses; Mmax from a laterally loaded pile program such as LPILE (Reese et al., 2005; Section 5.18). The check, from AASHTO (2002) 10.36 for steel, is fa/Fa + fb/[(1 - fa/F'e) Fb] <= 1.0 (Eq. 5-3), with fa = Pc/Acasing, fb = Mmax/S (S elastic section modulus of the casing), Fa = 0.47 Fy-casing and Fb = 0.55 Fy-casing (AASHTO Table 10.32.1.A), F'e the Euler buckling stress; the bar's bending contribution is ignored and Pc is conservatively carried by the casing alone. Section properties: Acasing = (pi/4)(OD^2 - ID^2) (Eq. 5-4a), S = Icasing/(OD/2) (Eq. 5-4b), Icasing = (pi/64)(OD^4 - ID^4) (Eq. 5-4c). F'e = pi^2 E / [FS (Kl/r)^2] (Eq. 5-5), E = 200,000 MPa (29,000 ksi), FS = 2.12, K = 1.0 (depends on end restraint, typically 1.0), L the unsupported length, r = (Icasing/Acasing)^(1/2). Carrying all axial load on the casing is conservative; Richards and Rothbauer (2004) proposed a check including the grout inside the casing, assuming negligible buckling: Pc/Pc-allowable + Mmax/Mallowable <= 1.0 (Eq. 5-6), Pc-allowable from Eq. 5-1, Mallowable = Fb (0.55 Fy-casing) x S. More advanced composite methods are beyond the scope of the manual.

sections.title: Step 6: Structural Design of Micropile Uncased Length
sections.summary: Uncased length: Pc-allowable = 0.4 f'c Agrout + 0.47 Fy-bar Abar (Eq. 5-7), bar yield not over 600 MPa (87 ksi) unless confined grout is shown to sustain more strain; Pt-allowable = 0.55 Fy-bar Abar (Eq. 5-8) with the actual bar yield. No combined stress check: the casing is extended deep enough that bending below it is negligible.
sections.body: (pp. 5-17 to 5-18) The allowable compression load for the uncased length is Pc-allowable = (0.4 f'c x Agrout + 0.47 Fy-bar x Abar) (Eq. 5-7). For the uncased portion the bar yield stress used in compression is assumed not to exceed 600 MPa (87 ksi), to prevent grout crushing at an assumed strain of 0.003 unless data show that the confined grout can sustain higher strain without crushing. The allowable tension load is Pt-allowable = 0.55 Fy-bar x Abar (Eq. 5-8), using the actual yield stress of the bar. A combined stress evaluation (Step 5 Part 3) is not performed for the uncased length, since micropiles are designed so that bending stresses are negligible there: the steel casing is placed deep enough that bending moments below it are negligible.
key_points: Eq. 5-7: Pc-allowable = 0.4 f'c Agrout + 0.47 Fy-bar Abar
Bar yield in compression not over 600 MPa (87 ksi) unless confined grout is shown to sustain higher strain
Eq. 5-8: Pt-allowable = 0.55 Fy-bar Abar, with the actual bar yield

sections.title: Establish Stratum for Bond Zone
sections.summary: Top loads are resisted by grout-to-ground bond over the bond zone (bond length), which can be formed in most soil and rock; design finds the length needed with a prescribed factor of safety. Review all borings for suitable strata and variations. As for ground anchors, generally unsuitable: organic soils and cohesive soils with average liquidity index above 0.2, liquid limit above 50 or plasticity index above 20, which may creep excessively; if used, test comprehensively and use higher factors of safety.
sections.body: (pp. 5-18 to 5-19) The maximum compression and tension loads at the top of the micropile must be resisted through grout-to-ground bond over a specific length, the bond zone or bond length, which can be formed in most soil and rock strata, the major differences being in the bond strength each ground type develops. The design objective is the bond zone length needed to resist the applied tension and compression with a prescribed factor of safety. All borings should be reviewed to identify strata appropriate for the bond zone and significant variations in subsurface conditions. Like ground anchors, certain deposits are not generally suitable for the bond zone: (1) organic soils; (2) cohesive soils with an average liquidity index greater than 0.2; (3) cohesive soils with an average liquid limit greater than 50; and (4) cohesive soils with an average plastic index greater than 20. Micropiles in these deposits may be susceptible to excessive creep at test and working loads; if they are used for the bond zone, comprehensive testing is recommended and higher factors of safety should be used (Section 5.9.2).

sections.title: Select Ultimate Bond Stress and Calculate Bond Length
sections.summary: PG-allowable = (alpha_bond/FS) pi Db Lb (Eq. 5-9); Lb = PG-allowable FS/(alpha_bond pi Db) (Eq. 5-10). Table 5-3 gives ultimate bond by ground and grout type; without local experience use no more than mid-range values, lower bound in loose granular or medium to high plasticity soils; assume Type A in rock and Type B in soil. FS = 2.0 with at least one ultimate or verification test before production, more in each different ground, and proof tests on about 5 percent of production piles; FS = 2.5 in creeping, high plasticity, weak rock or unfamiliar ground.
sections.body: (pp. 5-19 to 5-22) The allowable geotechnical bond capacity is PG-allowable = (alpha_bond / FS) x pi x Db x Lb (Eq. 5-9), where alpha_bond is the grout-to-ground ultimate bond strength, FS the factor of safety on it, Db the drill hole diameter and Lb the bond length. Usually Eq. 5-9 is rearranged to estimate the bond length for the maximum compression and/or tension (uplift) design load from Step 3: Lb = (PG-allowable x FS) / (alpha_bond x pi x Db) (Eq. 5-10). Table 5-3 (Summary of Typical alpha_bond (Grout-to-Ground Bond) Values for Micropile Design) gives ultimate grout-to-ground bond strengths for the four grouting methods (Types A to D) in various ground; for most micropile projects the contract documents give a minimum bond length based on Eq. 5-10. Unless the designer has experience in similar ground, values no greater than average (middle of the reported range) should be used, and lower bound values may be considered for loose granular materials or medium to high plasticity cohesive materials. Although the Contractor selects the specific type of micropile (Type A, B, C or D), the design engineer should assume a Type A micropile for bond zones in rock and a Type B micropile for bond zones in soil. Further sources: GEC No. 4 (FHWA-IF-99-015, 1999); PTI Recommendations for Prestressed Rock and Soil Anchors (2004); Ostermayer (1975); Xanthakos, Abramson and Bruce (1994); FHWA-RD-96-016 to -019 (1997); Tiebacks, FHWA/RD-82/047 (1982); Permanent Ground Anchors, FHWA-DP-68-1R (1988). For all highway projects some site-specific load testing of micropiles must be performed, and its scope defines the factor of safety applied to the ultimate bond strength for design. A factor of safety of 2.0 is recommended provided: at least one ultimate or verification test is run before production micropile installation, and one or more more in each significantly different ground type as construction proceeds (more for larger projects); and proof tests are run on a specified number of production piles, generally 5 percent of production micropiles (Chapter 7). Where the bond zone is in potentially creeping soils, high plasticity soils, weak rock, or other marginal ground or ground with limited experience, a factor of safety of 2.5 should be used for the bond length and as the basis for the maximum ultimate or verification test load; for micropiles in creep-susceptible soils, load testing includes measuring micropile deformation over an extended period at one or more loads, compared with a maximum allowable creep movement (Chapter 7).

sections.title: Evaluate Micropile Group Compression Capacity
sections.summary: Cohesive soils: efficiency 1.0 with the cap in firm contact or stiff ground (su > 95 kPa (1 tsf)), else 0.65 at s = 2.5 Db, 0.70 at 3.0 Db, 1.0 at 6.0 Db (Table 5-4); check block failure Qg = (2Bg + 2Lg) D su_avg + Bg Lg Nc su (Eqs. 5-11 to 5-13); allowable group capacity with FS 2.0. Cohesionless soils with s > 3 Db: sum of individual capacities (Eq. 5-14, eta = 1.0). Strong over weak soil: Qg/(Bg Lg) = qp <= qo + H/(10 Bg)(q1 - qo) <= q1 (Eq. 5-15; Meyerhof, 1976).
sections.body: (pp. 5-22 to 5-26) Micropile groups in cohesive soils: group efficiency depends on center-to-center spacing s and whether the cap bottom is in firm contact with the ground (Table 5-4): eta = 1.0 if the cap is in firm contact, or if not in contact but the ground is stiff (undrained shear strength greater than 95 kPa (1 tsf)); if not in contact and the ground is relatively soft (less than 95 kPa (1 tsf)) or disturbed, eta = 0.65 at s = 2.5 Db, 0.70 at 3.0 Db, 1.0 at 6.0 Db, interpolating between 0.70 and 1.0 for 3.0 Db < s < 6.0 Db. At small spacings block failure should be evaluated: for a group of width Bg, length Lg and depth D (Figure 5-3), Qg = (2Bg + 2Lg) D x su_avg + Bg Lg x Nc su (Eq. 5-11), su_avg being the average undrained shear strength along the penetration depth and su that at the base of the group, with no resistance from the cap; Nc = 5 (1 + 0.2 Bg/Lg)(1 + 0.2 D/Bg) for D/Bg <= 2.5 (Eq. 5-12) and Nc = 7.5 (1 + 0.2 Bg/Lg) for D/Lg > 2.5 (Eq. 5-13) (the print uses D/Bg in Eq. 5-12 and D/Lg in Eq. 5-13). Design group capacity: Step 1, ultimate group capacity Qg = (alpha_bond x pi x Db x Lb) x number of micropiles in group x eta (Eq. 5-14), eta from Table 5-4; Step 2, 'calculate ultimate group capacity according to Eq. 5-14' and use the lower value of Steps 1 and 2 (the print cites Eq. 5-14 in both steps); Step 3, use FS = 2.0 for the allowable group capacity. Micropile groups in cohesionless soils: with s greater than three grouted-body diameters (s > 3Db), group capacity is the sum of the individual resistances (Eq. 5-14 with eta = 1.0); e.g., pressure-grouted micropiles of typical 200 mm grouted diameter at typical minimum spacing of 750 to 1,000 mm need no group reduction. Micropile groups in strong soil overlying a weak or compressible soil: punching shear into the weaker layer should be checked by the method developed for drilled shaft groups (FHWA-IF-99-025, 1999): Qg/(Bg Lg) = qp <= qo + [H/(10 Bg)](q1 - qo) <= q1 (Eq. 5-15), where qo is the ultimate unit base resistance at the top of the lower (weaker) layer with its strength parameters, q1 that at the top of the upper (stronger) layer with its parameters, qp that at the micropile tips, and H the distance from the tips to the top of the weaker layer; for battered piles Bg and Lg are the plan dimensions at the pile bases; satisfying Eq. 5-15 should preclude punching (Figure 5-4).

sections.title: Evaluate Micropile Group Uplift Capacity
sections.summary: Uplift follows FHWA NHI-05-042 for driven piles. Cohesive soils: Qug = 2Z (X + Y) su_avg + Wg (Eq. 5-16, Figure 5-5), with FS 2.0. Cohesionless soils: effective weight of a soil block rising from the pile bases at 1H:4V, Qug = [(1/3)(Abase + Atop + sqrt(Abase Atop)) D] gamma (Eq. 5-17, Figure 5-6), Abase = Bg Lg, Atop = (Bg + D/2)(Lg + D/2), FS 1.0. Design on the lesser of group uplift and single-pile allowable uplift times the number of micropiles.
sections.body: (pp. 5-27 to 5-28) The design of micropile groups for uplift follows FHWA NHI-05-042 (2005) for uplift of driven piles in cohesionless and cohesive soils. Micropile groups in cohesive soils: the group uplift capacity may be calculated from the undrained shear strength of the block of soil enclosed by the group plus the effective weight of the cap and pile-soil block (Figure 5-5): Qug = 2Z x (X + Y) x su_avg + Wg (Eq. 5-16), where su_avg is the average undrained shear strength over the embedment depth along the group perimeter and Wg the effective weight of the pile/soil block including the cap; a factor of safety of 2.0 should be used for the allowable group uplift capacity. Micropile groups in cohesionless soils: the uplift capacity may conservatively be taken as the effective weight of a block of soil extending upward from the micropile bases at 1H:4V (Figure 5-6), the micropiles in the block conservatively weighing the same as the soil: Qug = [(1/3) x (Abase + Atop + sqrt(Abase x Atop)) x D] x gamma (Eq. 5-17), where Abase = Bg x Lg, Atop = (Bg + D/2) x (Lg + D/2) and gamma is the effective unit weight; the bracketed term is the volume of the enclosed soil. FS = 1.0 is acceptable here because the soil shear strength is conservatively neglected, so the allowable group capacity equals the Eq. 5-17 capacity. The allowable group uplift capacity (Eq. 5-16 or 5-17) should be compared with the allowable uplift capacity of a single micropile times the number of micropiles, and the design based on the lesser.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Driven pile group settlement methods generally apply to micropile groups. Total group settlement under the design load is the sum of (1) settlement of the ground in which the micropiles are built and (2) elastic compression or tension of an individual micropile, compared with the allowable settlement, which for typical highway bridges depends mainly on anticipated differential settlement between piers.
sections.body: (p. 5-29) In general, methods for estimating settlement of driven pile groups are applicable to micropile groups. The major components are (1) settlement of the ground in which the micropiles are constructed and (2) elastic compression/tension of an individual micropile; these are added to give the total settlement of the group under the design load, which is compared with the allowable settlement. The allowable value depends on the structure; for typical highway bridges the maximum vertical movement depends primarily on anticipated differential settlement between piers for single span or continuous span bridges.

sections.title: Micropile Group Settlement
sections.summary: As for driven piles (FHWA-NHI-05-042), the group load acts on an equivalent footing at two-thirds of the bond zone depth in the supporting layer (Figures 5-7, 5-8), or at 8/9 of the bond length over a clay just below the tips, spread at 1H:2V; the method is conservative. Cohesive soils: consolidation tests on undisturbed samples (GEC No. 5). Steps: footing location and size, pressure to where the increase is under 10 percent of effective overburden (design load), 1.5 to 3 m layers, settlement per layer. Cohesionless: dH = Ho (1/C') log[(po + dp)/po] (Eq. 5-18), C' from N160 (Figure 5-9).
sections.body: (pp. 5-29 to 5-35) Micropiles in a group can settle from consolidation of soil layers below the group, since a group distributes its load to the soil below; this should be considered where that soil is cohesive and subject to consolidation. The method is similar to that for driven piles (FHWA-NHI-05-042, 2005). For groups in soil (load transferred mainly by side resistance) the loads act on an equivalent footing at two-thirds of the embedment depth into the supporting layer, i.e., two-thirds of the bond zone depth (Figure 5-7, uniform soil; Figure 5-8, bond zone in a firm layer under a soft or weak layer, common for micropiles); where a clayey layer lies just below the tips, the equivalent footing is at 8/9 of the bond zone length. For vertical piles the footing plan area is the group perimeter. The load spreads within a frustum with 1H:2V side slopes, giving uniform added pressure at each level equal to the group load over the frustum base area, and settlements are calculated from the pressure increase in the underlying layers; the method is conservative, ignoring the added stiffness from the micropiles between the equivalent footing and the tips. Where clays may consolidate, undisturbed tube samples and consolidation tests should give compressibility and stress history (GEC No. 5); in cohesionless layers SPT data give compression parameters. Cohesive soils, Step 1: new load on the soil: (a) equivalent footing location (Figure 5-7 or 5-8); (b) dimensions, the group length and width for vertical piles, or the group plan at depth 2/3 D including batter; (c) pressure distribution down to where the increase is less than 10 percent of the existing effective overburden pressure, which sets the compressible thickness, using the group design load, not the ultimate; (d) sublayers 1.5 to 3 m (5 to 10 ft) thick, each of thickness H; (e) existing effective overburden po at each midpoint; (f) pressure increase dp at each midpoint. Step 2: consolidation test parameters. Step 3: settlement of each layer by an appropriate equation, summed. Cohesionless soils give only immediate settlement: Step 1 as above (a to f); Step 2: average corrected (overburden and hammer efficiency) N160 for each layer and bearing capacity index C' from Figure 5-9; Step 3: dH = Ho (1/C') log[(po + dp)/po] (Eq. 5-18), summed over the layers. In layered profiles the cohesive and cohesionless methods are applied to the appropriate layers and the settlements added.

sections.title: Micropile Elastic Movement
sections.summary: Elastic movement of one micropile is added to the group ground settlement: delta = PL/AE (Eq. 5-19), or the sum of Pi Li/(Ai Ei) over segments (Eq. 5-20). Compression: EA = Agrout Egrout + Asteel Esteel (Eq. 5-21); tension: EA = Asteel Esteel (Eq. 5-22); Egrout (MPa) = 4732 (f'c (MPa))^(1/2). Conservatively take the full design load over the length above the bond zone and over one-half the bond length; for micropiles bonded in or bearing on rock use the full length above rock. Cyclic load tests can confirm the elastic lengths.
sections.body: (pp. 5-36 to 5-37) The elastic compression and/or tension of a single micropile under the design load is added to the group settlement from Section 5.10.2 to give the total estimated group settlement. It depends on the load, pile stiffness and load transfer to the ground through grout-to-ground bond. In general form: delta_elastic = PL/AE (Eq. 5-19), with P the design load at the ground surface (kN), L the pile length (m), A the section area (m2) and E the section modulus (kPa). Because stiffness may vary along the pile and load is transferred to the ground, the displacement may be summed over n segments: delta_elastic = sum(i = 1 to n) Pi Li/(Ai Ei) (Eq. 5-20), with Li, Ai and Ei the length, average area and average modulus of each segment and Pi its average axial load, falling from the full load at the top to the mobilized end bearing at the tip. Stiffness AE is complex because the grout contributes in compression and reinforcement may vary (casing and perhaps bar above, bar below). For compression, EApile = [Agrout x Egrout] + [Asteel x Esteel] (Eq. 5-21); for tension, EApile = [Asteel x Esteel] (Eq. 5-22). Egrout is quite variable but may be estimated as Egrout (MPa) = 4732 x (f'c (MPa))^(1/2) (Egrout (ksi) = 57 x (f'c (psi))^(1/2)). Conservatively, no load is transferred to the ground above the top of the bond zone, so that length compresses per Eq. 5-19 with P the design load and L the length above the bond zone (Eq. 5-20 with segments where the section changes). In the bond zone, with usually constant section and the design load assumed carried uniformly in side resistance, use Eq. 5-19 with P the design load and L one-half the bond length. For micropiles bonded in rock or end bearing on rock, assume the full length above the top of rock. The assumed elastic lengths can be confirmed by load tests with incremental load cycles (like a ground anchor performance test). An example is in Sample Problem No. 1.

sections.title: Step 10. Design Micropile Connection at Pile Cap
sections.summary: A pile cap spreads loads and moments to the micropiles (cap design per AASHTO, not covered). Figures 5-10 to 5-13 show tension and compression connections: top bearing plate with stiffeners welded to the casing (5-10, as in Sample Problem No. 1); casing with welded shear rings in non-shrink grout in a cored hole through an existing footing, with chipped grooves 20 mm deep and 32 mm wide (5-11; load test required); bearing on pile top and bar plate (5-12); bar cast in the footing (5-13). Figures 5-14 to 5-16 show compression-only connections.
sections.body: (pp. 5-38 to 5-44) Unless a single micropile carries a load, a pile cap (footing) spreads structure loads and overturning moments to the group; reinforced concrete caps are designed per the AASHTO Standard Specifications, individual DOTs may set minimums (cover, pile embedment), and cap structural design is not addressed in the manual. The connection depends on the required capacity, reinforcement type and cap details; seven examples are shown, Figures 5-10 to 5-13 for piles with tension and compression and Figures 5-14 to 5-16 for compression only. Figure 5-10: composite micropile in a new or extended footing; load passes through the top bearing plate, with stiffener plates adding plate bending strength and weld length (omit if not needed); the bar's share of tension can pass to the plate through the nut, casing-to-concrete bond can reduce the plate and weld demand, and part of the compression can pass by bearing if the bearing surface is fabricated to higher quality; Sample Problem No. 1 designs a similar connection without these refinements. Figure 5-11: composite micropile through an oversized hole cored in an existing footing or slab; the annulus is cleaned (usually pressure washing) and filled with non-shrink cement grout; steel rings welded to the casing transfer load to the grout, spaced to avoid combining bearing stresses; capacity is the sum of ring bearing, grout-to-existing-concrete transfer and existing concrete shear; grooves chipped into the core hole (typically 20 mm deep and 32 mm wide (3/4 in. by 1-1/4 in.)) and drilled-and-epoxied vertical bars can add capacity; rings and grooves may be omitted in thick footings; the Contractor should load test, give previous test data or in-house testing to show the connection supports the design load. Figure 5-12: composite micropile in a new footing; compression by bearing on the pile top and bar plate, tension by bearing on the bar plate, part by casing-to-concrete bond. Figure 5-13: bar-reinforced micropile cast into a new footing, load by bearing on the bar plate and bar bond; the construction joint between pile grout and footing concrete is an important quality item. Figure 5-14: compression connection for moderate loads where concrete bearing on the pile top is within AASHTO limits (Section 8.15.2.1.3); Figure 5-15: heavy loads needing a bearing plate welded to the casing; Figure 5-16: compression pile through an existing footing, the grout bond depending on methods (cored or down-the-hole hammered hole) and materials; connection load tests are appropriate.

sections.title: Step 11. Develop Load Testing Program
sections.summary: The load testing program (Section 7.6) must match the factor of safety on bond; the Section 5.9.2 minimum verification and proof testing corresponds to FS 2.0. sections.body: (pp. 5-44 to 5-45) Section 7.6 gives the evaluations for developing a load testing program. Of primary importance, the scope must be consistent with the factor of safety selected for grout-ground bond; the minimum verification and proof testing in Section 5.9.2 is consistent with a factor of safety of 2.0. Maximum test loads should not exceed 80 percent of the ultimate structural capacity of the micropile: Pult-compression = [0.85 f'c-grout x Agrout + fy-casing x Acasing + fy-bar x Abar] (Eq. 5-23) and Pult-tension = [fy-casing x Acasing + fy-bar x Abar] (Eq. 5-24). sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Corrosion protection of metallic components is needed for long-term durability; its degree depends on loading, service life, ground aggressiveness, structure importance and consequences of failure, and the Project Designer selects it for each micropile. High corrosion potential is indicated by low resistivity, high chlorides or sulfides, too low or too high pH, high saturation and stray currents. Grout degradation by sulfate, chloride or acid attack should also be considered (FHWA-NHI-05-042).
sections.body: (pp. 5-45 to 5-46) Protecting the metallic components of a micropile against corrosion is necessary for adequate long-term durability. The degree and extent of protection depends on the loading condition, expected service life, aggressiveness of the ground, perceived importance of the structure and consequences of failure; in all cases the Project Designer is responsible for selecting the corrosion protection for each micropile. Variables indicating high corrosion potential: low ground resistivity; high concentration of chlorides or sulfides in ground or groundwater; too low or too high pH of ground or groundwater; high saturation; and stray currents. Together they define the ground corrosion potential (aggressivity). Potential degradation of the cement grout by sulfate, chloride and/or acid attack should also be considered; information on cement degradation for pile design is in FHWA-NHI-05-042.
key_points: Degree of protection depends on loading, service life, ground aggressiveness, structure importance and consequences of failure
The Project Designer selects the corrosion protection for each micropile

sections.title: Evaluation of Soil Corrosion Potential
sections.summary: Ground is aggressive (strong corrosion potential) if any Table 5-5 limit is exceeded during the service life: pH below 5 or above 10 (AASHTO T 289), resistivity below 3,000 ohm-cm (T 288), sulfates above 200 ppm (T 290), chlorides above 100 ppm (T 291) (Elias et al., 2001). Corroding adjacent buried structures may also indicate it. Without tests, assume aggressive ground; consider future changes (mining, chemical plants or storage).
sections.body: (p. 5-46) Tests in Table 5-5 classify the corrosion potential of the ground (Elias et al., 2001): strong corrosion potential (aggressive) where pH is less than 5 or greater than 10 (AASHTO T 289), resistivity is less than 3,000 ohm-cm (T 288), sulfates exceed 200 ppm (T 290) or chlorides exceed 100 ppm (T 291). In general the ground is classified as aggressive if any one condition exceeds its limit during the service life of the micropile. Buried structures immediately adjacent to the project showing corrosion or direct chemical attack may also indicate strong corrosion potential. If tests are not performed, the ground should be assumed aggressive. Classification should consider possible changes during the service life that may make the ground aggressive (e.g., near mining operations, chemical plants or chemical storage areas).

sections.title: Methods for Corrosion Protection of Reinforcing Steel
sections.summary: Protection is physical (a continuous barrier), chemical (sacrificial or dielectric material) or both. Grout protection: centralized bar fully covered by neat cement grout, giving an alkaline environment (Figure 5-17(a)). Epoxy coating: fusion-bonded, typically at least 12 mils (0.3 mm), thicker may reduce bond, field-patched (ASTM A775/AASHTO M282). Galvanizing: hot-dip zinc per ASTM A153, not on high strength bars. Encapsulation: corrugated PVC (at least 1 mm) or HDPE (at least 1.5 mm) sheath, grout-filled, gives double corrosion protection (PTI, 2004).
sections.body: (pp. 5-46 to 5-48) Corrosion protection may be physical, a continuous barrier between the bar, casing or other metal parts and the corrosion sources, or chemical, a sacrificial or dielectric material that precludes electric current flow, or a combination. The most common micropile systems: Grout protection: the bar is fully covered with neat cement grout, with centralizers along the bar (Figure 5-17(a)) ensuring cover to the borehole wall; the grout provides an alkaline environment that reduces corrosion potential. Epoxy coating: fusion-bonded epoxy applied by the manufacturer, minimum thickness typically 12 mils (0.3 mm); thicker coatings may reduce steel-to-grout bond; epoxy gives physical and chemical (dielectric) protection; damage in transport and handling is commonly patched by field spraying; standards and allowable damage are in ASTM A775/AASHTO M282, and patching materials should be approved by the coating manufacturer and inert in cement grout. Galvanized coating: hot-dip zinc forming a protective zinc oxide layer, physical and chemical; galvanization shall meet ASTM A153 and should not be used on high strength bars. Encapsulation: for maximum protection, a corrugated PVC (minimum 1 mm (0.04 in.)) or HDPE (minimum 1.5 mm (0.06 in.)) sheath around the bar, as for permanent ground anchors; corrugations transfer load to the grout, and grout-filled corrugated sheaths give double corrosion protection; used with DSI threadbar, GEWI bar (Figure 5-17(b)) and others, and shall meet the PTI (2004) encapsulation requirements for ground anchors.

Galvanizing: hot-dip zinc per ASTM A153; not on high strength bars

sections.title: Methods for Corrosion Protection of Steel Casing
sections.summary: Grout outside the casing gives no quantifiable protection, and coatings on drill casing are impractical (abraded by soil). Casing in compression in aggressive ground is protected by a sacrificial steel thickness in design; casing should not carry tension in aggressive ground. Figure 5-17 shows GEWI piles with grout protection only and with double corrosion protection.
sections.body: (pp. 5-48 to 5-49) Grout that may fill the annulus outside the steel casing is not considered sufficient to provide a quantifiable level of corrosion protection. Corrosion resistant coatings on permanent drill casing are impractical because the abrasive action of the soil would likely damage them. Corrosion protection for casing in compression in aggressive environments is typically provided by including a sacrificial steel thickness in the design, and casing should not be used to carry tension loads in aggressive ground (Figure 5-17 shows GEWI piles with standard and double corrosion protection).

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Requirements for Micropiles
sections.summary: Table 5-6 (after DFI, 2004): tension in aggressive ground, do not rely on casing, and coat, galvanize or encapsulate the bar plus grout cover; tension in non-aggressive ground, casing needs nothing if tension is under 20 percent of thread strength; compression in aggressive ground, at least 1.6 mm (0.063 in.) outside casing loss (AASHTO 4.5.7.4) plus grout cover. CCTG (1992) gives 2 to 5 mm for 75 years in moderately to strongly corrosive ground; site-specific corrosivity studies are strongly recommended in aggressive ground.
sections.body: (pp. 5-50 to 5-51) Corrosion protection recommendations are in Table 5-6 (after DFI, 2004). Tension, aggressive ground: do not rely on casing for load capacity; bar epoxy coated, galvanized or encapsulated in a plastic sheath, and grout cover. Tension, non-aggressive ground: casing needs no protection if its tension load is less than 20 percent of casing thread strength, or do not rely on casing; bar bare (not recommended for permanent or cyclic tension), epoxy coated, galvanized or encapsulated, and grout cover. Compression, aggressive ground: casing with minimum 1.6 mm (0.063 in.) corrosion loss on the outside; bar with grout cover, the Specifier possibly adding the tension options. Compression, non-aggressive ground: casing none, bar grout cover. The Specifier may use different corrosion losses from site-specific studies. Notes: tension means permanent tension or temporary tension (e.g., wind, seismic, impact) on critical structures; for temporary tension on normal structures compression protection may be used; tension protection also applies to the length in tension from lateral loads and/or overturning moments; protection must extend 5 m (15 ft) below corrosive material; core steel protection must extend at least 1.5 m (5 ft) into the casing; minimum grout cover 1 inch in soil and 0.5 inch in rock, or 0.25 inch in soil or rock with protective coatings in compression. The 1.6 mm (0.063 in.) minimum casing loss in aggressive ground is the AASHTO Section 4.5.7.4 reduction for concrete-filled pipe piles. CCTG (1992) guidance for a 75-year design life gives losses of 2 mm (0.0787 in.) to 5 mm (printed '0.196 mm') for non-protected steel in moderately to strongly corrosive environments without site corrosivity studies, more for longer lives. Because these sources give a wide range, site-specific corrosivity studies are strongly recommended where micropiles will be in aggressive ground (Table 5-5).

sections.title: Plunge Length
sections.summary: With a casing plunge length into the bond zone (Figure 5-1; mainly for bond zones in soil), part of the load transfers to the ground through the cased portion, reducing the load on the uncased length (Figure 5-18): Ptransfer-allowable = (alpha_bond/FS) pi Db (Plunge Length) (Eq. 5-25), alpha_bond from Table 5-3. Achieving it depends on casing installation, soil and grouting, so confirm it by site-specific load testing, or conservatively neglect Ptransfer.
sections.body: (pp. 5-51 to 5-52) The micropile in Figure 5-1 has a casing plunge length. With this detail, used primarily for bond zones in soil, part of the design load is assumed to transfer to the surrounding ground over the plunge length through the cased portion, reducing the load on the uncased portion (Figure 5-18) and allowing less steel through the uncased length; the reduction is the transfer load Ptransfer. The allowable axial load transferred through the plunge length is Ptransfer-allowable = (alpha_bond / FS) x pi x Db x (Plunge Length) (Eq. 5-25), with the unit grout-to-ground bond alpha_bond (Table 5-3) acting uniformly over the plunge length. Reliably achieving it depends on the casing installation method, soil type and grouting method giving sufficient grout coverage between casing and ground, so designs using a plunge length and reduced load on the uncased portion should be confirmed by site-specific load testing in which transfer over the plunge length is measured or computed from verification tests; alternatively Ptransfer may be conservatively neglected.

sections.title: End Bearing Micropiles
sections.summary: End bearing is generally negligible for micropiles in soil or weak rock, but micropiles on high quality sound rock may carry load mainly in end bearing. Ensure the pile is not on a boulder or over voids or soft material, with exploration detailed enough to judge rock quality (Table 5-2). Design as for end bearing drilled shafts or from load test experience; a nominal rock socket of about 0.6 m (2 ft) confirms founding on rock; capacity will likely be controlled by structural capacity.
sections.body: (pp. 5-52 to 5-53) Because of their small cross section, end bearing is generally considered negligible for micropiles in soil or weak rock. Micropiles founded on high quality sound rock, however, may develop capacity primarily through end bearing and secondarily by side resistance; care must be taken that the micropile is not terminated on a boulder or on rock with voids or very soft material below, and the subsurface investigation should be detailed enough to determine rock quality (Table 5-2). Design may be similar to end bearing drilled shafts or based on load test experience with similar micropiles. Typically a nominal rock socket (on the order of 0.6 m (2 ft)) is used to assure founding on high quality rock. The capacity of end bearing micropiles on competent rock will likely be controlled by the structural capacity, since very high end bearing can be achieved on rock.

sections.title: Downdrag
sections.summary: Downdrag adds compression when soil around the cased length settles relative to the micropile (methods in FHWA-NHI-05-042 and FHWA-IF-99-025); consider it with compressible silts, clays or peats, recent fill, or lowered groundwater. Conservatively take downdrag from the ground surface to the top of the bond zone using Table 5-3 bond values for the grouting used; check structural capacity for downdrag plus top load at the top of the bond zone. Small surface area limits downdrag; an oversized outer casing can isolate the pile; avoid battered micropiles where large settlement is expected.
sections.body: (pp. 5-53 to 5-54) Micropiles may carry additional compression from downdrag when soils in contact with the cased portion (above the bond zone) move down relative to the micropile and drag it downward, adding to the structure load; background and methods are in FHWA-NHI-05-042 (driven piles) and FHWA-IF-99-025 (drilled shafts). Downdrag can develop where surface soils can settle and the element passes through them into relatively rigid geomaterial; it should be considered where (1) the site is underlain by compressible silts, clays or peats, (2) fill has recently been placed, or (3) groundwater is substantially lowered. If surface soils move down more than the micropile, a conservative solution assumes downdrag along the micropile from the ground surface to the top of the bond zone, computed with Table 5-3 bond stresses considering the grouting technique over the weak materials; the maximum load, at the top of the bond zone, is the downdrag plus the top load, and structural capacity is checked for this total. Micropiles have benefits where downdrag is a concern: their small surface area gives relatively small downdrag forces, and an additional oversized outer casing through the settling soils can further isolate them. Battered micropiles should not be used where large settlements are expected because of the added bending.

sections.title: Analysis Steps for Single Laterally Loaded Micropile
sections.summary: Steps: (1) pile inputs; (2) segments with uniform section, the bar's lateral resistance negligible and moments usually negligible below about 20 diameters, setting the minimum cased length; (3) layers; (4) soil parameters, e50 and k (Tables 5-7 to 5-10), with good strength data in the upper 5 m (15 ft); (5) loads and head fixity: check strength for the larger moment of pinned and fixed heads, deflection with representative fixity (Table 5-11); (6) combined stress (Eq. 5-3 or 5-6); (7) deflection acceptability.
sections.body: (pp. 5-54 to 5-60) Step 1: basic inputs: pile length; elastic moduli of grout, bar and casing; distance from pile head to ground surface; ground slope. Step 2: divide the micropile into segments of uniform section with diameter, moment of inertia and area; a laterally loaded micropile has a cased upper length; a center bar along the whole length gives negligible lateral resistance; lateral loads and moments at the ground surface are usually carried from the surface to a depth on the order of 20 diameters, below which moments are usually negligible; the analyzed length should make moments, shears and movement negligible at the bottom, and can set the minimum cased length. Step 3: delineate soil/rock layers over the maximum trial penetration. Step 4: soil inputs: effective unit weight and undrained shear strength for cohesive layers, effective unit weight and drained friction angle for cohesionless layers, plus e50 (axial strain at half the shear strength, clays only) and k (slope of soil resistance versus deflection), typically from Tables 5-7 to 5-10. User-defined p-y curves may be used from micropile lateral load tests in similar ground (with deflections measured at the ground line and along the pile); actual foundation displacements will likely be less than in load tests, which lack cap stiffness and embedment. Most engineers use the p-y curves in programs such as LPILE, not developed for small-diameter micropiles but reasonably accurate; good characterization of the upper 5 m (15 ft) is critical (Richards and Rothbauer, 2004), and overly conservative near-surface strengths will significantly overpredict ground line movement, so site-specific strength data should be obtained. Step 5: critical load combinations and boundary conditions (axial load, lateral load and moment at the ground line); full head fixity gives large negative moments at the top and small deflections, a pinned head the largest moment below ground and larger deflections; little data exists on fixity for vertical micropile connections, so typical practice checks structural capacity for the larger maximum moment from pinned (0 percent) and fixed (100 percent) analyses, while ground line deflections use a representative fixity consistent with, and achieved by, the as-built connection (Table 5-11; greater fixity may be achievable, assessed per project). 50 percent fixity in LPILE: run 100 percent fixity (zero head slope) to get Mneg (100%) at the ground line, then a second run with a moment boundary condition of 50 percent of Mneg (100%) for the ground line deflection (examples Figures 5-19, 5-20; Sample Problem No. 2 applies the combined stress check, printed as Eqs. 5-4 and 5-6). Step 6: check structural capacity for combined axial and bending by Eq. 5-3 or Eq. 5-6, conservatively with the casing alone carrying the moment and ignoring threaded connection weakness (see Sections 5.5.3 and 5.18.3); if not met, add an oversized casing at the top, enlarge the top diameter, embed the cap deeper for more passive resistance, or batter some micropiles, evaluated per project (some options may be outside the contractor's control). Step 7: judge acceptability by deflection under the design load and modify section properties as needed.

Center bar gives negligible lateral resistance; moments usually negligible below about 20 diameters, which sets the minimum cased length

Table 5-11: casing embedment 300 mm (12 in.) or less = 0 %; 450 mm (18 in.) = 50 %; 600 mm (24 in.) or more = 100 % (footing restrained)
50 % fixity in LPILE: second run with head moment = 50 % of Mneg from the fixed-head run
Step 6: combined stress (Eq. 5-3 or 5-6); if inadequate, oversized top casing, larger top diameter, deeper cap or batter piles

sections.title: Evaluation of Micropile Lateral Load Capacity at Threaded Casing Joints
sections.summary: Conservatively take the wall at a threaded joint as 50 percent of the intact wall, so the joint OD is OD - tw: Sjoint = Ijoint/[(OD - tw)/2] = (pi/64)[(OD - tw)^4 - ID^4]/[(OD - tw)/2] (Eq. 5-26). From Eq. 5-3, Mmax(joint) = Sjoint (1 - fa/Fa)(1 - fa/F'e) Fb (Eq. 5-27). Demonstrated in Sample Problem No. 2.
sections.body: (pp. 5-60 to 5-61) A conservative approach evaluates the bending moment capacity at a threaded casing joint by assuming the casing wall thickness at the joint is 50 percent of the intact wall thickness tw, reducing the section modulus; the joint outside diameter is then OD - 2(tw/2) = OD - tw, and Sjoint = Ijoint / [(OD - tw)/2] = (pi/64) x [(OD - tw)^4 - ID^4] / [(OD - tw)/2] (Eq. 5-26). Eq. 5-3 then gives the maximum bending moment at a joint: Mmax(joint) = Sjoint x (1 - fa/Fa) x (1 - fa/F'e) Fb (Eq. 5-27). The method is demonstrated in Sample Problem No. 2.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Group deflection may be 2 to 3 times that of a single pile at the same intensity; trailing rows resist less (Holloway et al., 1981; Brown et al., 1988), so group efficiency is below 1. FOREVER (2003): group effects negligible for in-line micropiles at 6 to 7 diameters and for rows perpendicular to loading just over 3 diameters. Brown et al. (printed 1998) p-multipliers: in a 3 by 3 group in very dense sand at 3b, Pm = 0.8 lead, 0.4 middle, 0.3 back row (Figure 5-21); FOREVER suggests slightly higher Pm for micropiles (limited centrifuge data).
sections.body: (pp. 5-61 to 5-62) As for other piles, micropile group behavior depends on spacing. Group deflection under lateral load may be 2 to 3 times that of a single pile loaded to the same intensity. Holloway et al. (1981) and Brown et al. (1988) reported that piles in trailing rows have significantly less lateral resistance than lead row piles and deflect more, because of pile-soil-pile interaction, so the group lateral capacity is less than the sum of the individual capacities (group efficiency less than 1). Experiments in the FOREVER National Project (FOREVER, 2003) on horizontally loaded micropile groups concluded that group effects are negligible for in-line micropiles at spacings of 6 to 7 diameters, and for micropiles in a row perpendicular to the loading at spacings just greater than 3 diameters. The lateral capacity of a pile in a group depends on its position and the spacing. Brown et al. (printed 1998) proposed a p-multiplier Pm applied to all p-y curves of piles in a given row (Figure 5-21); in a lateral load test of a 3 by 3 group in very dense sand at 3b spacing, Brown found Pm = 0.8 for the leading row, and 0.4 and 0.3 for the middle and back rows. Further driven pile group studies are summarized in FHWA-NHI-05-042 (2005); preliminary FOREVER results suggest micropile Pm values may be slightly higher than those recommended, but only limited centrifuge data are available. Brown and Bollman (1993) proposed the p-multiplier design procedure outlined in 5.19.2, which may be used for micropile groups.

sections.title: Step By Step Design Procedure For Laterally Loaded Pile Groups
sections.summary: Step 1: single pile p-y curves. Step 2: LPILE runs with Pm = 0.8 (lead row), 0.4 (second) and 0.3 (third and later), reasonable at 3-diameter spacing and ground line deflections of 10 to 15 percent of diameter and conservative for larger spacing or smaller deflection; plot load-deflection per row (Figure 5-22(a)). Step 3: group deflection from the average curve at load per pile. Step 4: moment per row at that deflection (Figure 5-22(b)), checked by Eq. 5-3 or 5-6. Step 5: refined superstructure-substructure evaluation (FHWA-NHI-05-042 Appendix F.8).
sections.body: (pp. 5-62 to 5-65) Step 1: develop p-y curves for a single pile (guidance above). Step 2: LPILE analyses: (a) using the Pm for each row position, develop load-deflection and load-moment data; (b) Pm values of 0.8 for the lead row, 0.4 for the second row and 0.3 for the third and subsequent rows are suggested, reasonable for center-to-center spacing of three diameters and ground surface deflections of 10 to 15 percent of the micropile diameter, and conservative for larger spacings or smaller deflections (as anticipated for typical micropile groups); (c) determine ground line shear load versus head deflection for each row (Figure 5-22(a)) by running a set of shear loads. Step 3: estimate group deflection: (a) average the load at a given deflection over all piles for the group response (Figure 5-22(a)); (b) divide the group lateral load by the number of piles and enter the group average curve with that load per pile to estimate the group deflection. Step 4: structural acceptability: (a) plot maximum bending moment versus deflection for each row (Figure 5-22(b)); (b) at the estimated group deflection read the maximum moment for a pile in each row and check by Eq. 5-3 or Eq. 5-6. Step 5: refined group evaluation considering superstructure-substructure interaction; a detailed driven pile group example is in Appendix F.8 of FHWA-NHI-05-042 (2005), with the same steps for micropile groups.

sections.title: Soil-Structure Interaction Analyses for Micropile Groups
sections.summary: Micropiles are often combined with existing deep foundations, so load sharing must be estimated; statically indeterminate cases need the stiffness of existing elements, micropiles and cap. FB-Pier (2001), developed with FHWA support, is a nonlinear finite element soil-structure interaction program using p-multipliers for axial, lateral and combined loads; GROUP (2003) can also be used.
sections.body: (p. 5-66) The methods above evaluate group lateral response from single micropile analyses. Micropiles are often used with existing deep foundation elements, so the load shared by each element must be estimated; this may be statically indeterminate (e.g., more than 2 piles in a cross section), requiring the stiffness of the existing elements, new micropiles and pile cap in the analysis. FB-Pier (2001), developed with FHWA support as the primary design tool for pile groups under axial and lateral loads, is a nonlinear finite element soil-structure interaction program using a p-multiplier approach for axial, lateral and combined loads (http://bsi-web.ce.ufl.edu). GROUP (2003) can also model pile groups (www.ensoftinc.com).
key_points: Micropiles with existing foundations need load sharing estimates; indeterminate cases need element and cap stiffness
FB-Pier (2001): FHWA-supported nonlinear finite element soil-structure interaction program with p-multipliers
GROUP (2003) can also model pile groups
sections.applicability: Programs for groups with mixed or statically indeterminate foundation elements.

sections.title: Battered Micropiles
sections.summary: Vertical micropiles have limited lateral capacity; battering adds resistance at little extra cost per length. Lateral capacity of battered micropiles (Sample Problem No. 1) is summed and compared with the applied lateral load, any remainder carried in bending by LPILE analysis. Groups with vertical and battered piles need soil-structure interaction analysis (5.19.3). Battered groups are stiffer but put larger moments in the cap (a concern in highly seismic regions); avoid them where ground may settle around them (Section 5.21).
sections.body: (pp. 5-66 to 5-67) The lateral capacity of individual vertical micropiles is limited compared with drilled shafts and driven piles, and as with other systems micropiles can be battered for additional lateral resistance; since micropile drilling equipment drills vertically and subvertically, battered micropiles cost little more per unit length and are of similar quality. The lateral capacity of a single battered micropile is calculated in Sample Problem No. 1; the total lateral capacity of the battered micropiles is the sum of their capacities, compared with the superstructure lateral load, and any remainder is carried by the micropiles in bending (used in an LPILE analysis). Groups with vertical and battered piles should be analyzed with the soil-structure interaction programs of Section 5.19.3. Groups with battered piles are relatively stiff and move less laterally than the same number of vertical piles, but the stiffness gives greater bending moments in the pile cap, a concern especially in highly seismic regions. Battered micropiles should not be used where ground settlement around them is possible, since settlement induces added bending and some loss of support (seismic regions, Section 5.21).
key_points: Vertical micropiles have limited lateral capacity; battering adds resistance at little extra cost per length
Battered micropile lateral capacities are summed and compared with the applied lateral load; remainder carried in bending (LPILE)
Groups of vertical and battered piles need soil-structure interaction analysis (Section 5.19.3)
Battered groups move less but put larger bending moments in the cap (concern in highly seismic regions)
Do not use battered micropiles where ground may settle around them

sections.title: Buckling Considerations for Micropiles
sections.summary: Buckling may control where soft or weak soils, voids or liquefiable soils overlie the bearing strata (Cadden and Gomez, 2002). Casing only: Pcr = pi^2 EI/l^2 + Es l^2/pi^2 (Eq. 5-28); Es_LIMIT = 1/[(4I/A^2)(E/Fy^2)] (Eq. 5-29). If Es_LIMIT < Es, buckling need not be considered; otherwise Pc-allowable = Eq. 5-1 x Fa/(0.47 Fy-steel) (Eq. 5-30), Fa from Eqs. 5-31 and 5-32 (FS 2.12, K 1.0, l = weak layer thickness or scour depth). Es from Tables 5-12, 5-13; Figure 5-23. The print numbers these subsections 5.21.1 and 5.21.2.
sections.body: (pp. 5-67 to 5-71) Printed '5.21.1 General' (p. 5-67): because micropiles are often installed to or into sound rock or dense/hard soil, their capacity is often set by structural strength rather than side resistance. Lateral restraint from the ground reduces buckling potential, but where soft or weak soils (e.g., very soft sedimentary deposits), voids (e.g., karst) or liquefiable soils overlie the bearing strata, buckling may control and should be considered; the subsurface investigation must identify these zones and their depths should be recorded during installation. A more detailed treatment is in Cadden and Gomez (2002). Printed '5.21.2 Micropile Surrounded by Very Weak or Liquefiable Soil' (pp. 5-67 to 5-71): very weak or liquefiable soil cannot be defined by a parameter such as SPT N for buckling, so a simple analysis compares the critical buckling load Pcr with the micropile capacity using a soil modulus, counting only the steel casing (grout inside and outside ignored): Pcr = pi^2 EI/l^2 + Es l^2/pi^2 (Eq. 5-28), with E the casing modulus (e.g., 200,000 MPa (29,000 ksi)), I the moment of inertia (Eq. 5-4), l the unsupported length taken as the thickness of the weak or potentially liquefiable soil, and Es the lateral reaction modulus of the soil over that length. The limiting modulus for buckling is Es_LIMIT = 1 / [(4I/A^2)(E/Fy^2)] (Eq. 5-29), the first bracketed term geometric and the second material, together the pile factor in units of stress^-1. If Es_LIMIT is less than the measured or assumed Es, geotechnical and structural strength control and buckling needs no further consideration; if Es_LIMIT exceeds Es, buckling should be evaluated further. Es ranges are in Tables 5-12 and 5-13, and Figure 5-23 charts limiting moduli for micropile materials. Where buckling is possible, the allowable compression of the cased section is Eq. 5-1 modified: Pc-allowable = [0.4 f'c-grout x Agrout + 0.47 Fy-steel (Abar + Acasing)] x Fa/(0.47 Fy-steel) (Eq. 5-30), with Fa = (Fy-steel/FS) x [1 - (Kl/rt)^2/(2 Cc^2)] if 0 < Kl/rt <= Cc (Eq. 5-31) and Fa = pi^2 Esteel/(FS [Kl/rt]^2) if Kl/rt > Cc (Eq. 5-32), where Cc = sqrt(2 pi^2 Esteel/Fy-steel), K = 1.0 (Section 5.6), l the unsupported length, rt = (I/A)^(1/2) for the steel section only, FS = 2.12 (AASHTO (2002) Table 10.32.1.A) and Fy-steel the casing yield stress. The unsupported length is the thickness of weak soil around the micropile, with K conservatively 1.0, and the analysis can treat scour with the scour depth as the unsupported length. Where combined axial and bending stresses exist and buckling should be checked, Eq. 5-3 should be used.

sections.title: Micropiles Installed through Voids
sections.summary: A micropile through a void (Figure 5-24) is checked with Eq. 5-30, the void length analyzed as pinned-pinned, pinned-fixed or fixed-fixed; grouted only along the bond length with a gap around the casing, take it as pinned at both ends (k = 1.0). If fixed in hard rock above the void, only vertical load passes over the void, so assuming lateral transfer is conservative. Check joints with Eq. 5-29 using Ijoint (Eq. 5-26), conservatively; in karst design for buckling with joints or add continuous internal reinforcement across voids or very soft soil.
sections.body: (pp. 5-72 to 5-73) Figure 5-24 shows a micropile installed through a void, such as in karst, with a centered load P at the top and consistent ground over its length except at the void. Its structural capacity should be checked with Eq. 5-30; depending on the installation procedure, the portion through the void may be analyzed as a doubly pinned, pinned-fixed or fixed-fixed column with k selected accordingly. The model assumes grout only along the bond length and an annular gap around the casing over the unbonded length, so the micropile can conservatively be taken as pinned at both ends (k = 1.0). Where the pile passes through hard rock above the void, consider whether lateral loads or moments can reach the portion in the void; if the pile is fixed in rock above the void, no lateral load is transferred over the void length, only vertical load, so the allowable load assuming lateral transfer is conservative. Micropiles may be susceptible to buckling failure at casing joints: use Eq. 5-29 with a reduced moment of inertia calculated as Ijoint in Eq. 5-26, conservative since it assumes joint stiffness over the whole unsupported length; more detailed analyses using reduced stiffness only at the joint are complex and beyond the scope. As a practical matter, micropiles through karst must be designed for buckling considering casing joints, or include continuous internal reinforcement along portions crossing voids or very soft or loose soil.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Micropiles are added to existing foundations in seismic retrofits for overturning, uplift and lateral forces; guidance is AASHTO (2002) Division I-A and JPWRI (2002). Seismic response involves three forces and three moments (Figure 5-25). Pseudo-static or dynamic analysis models the pile as a beam-column on nonlinear lateral (p-y) and axial (t-z) springs; torsion is usually ignored for highway bridges. t-z curves: Lam and Martin (1986, 1997), Kraft et al. (1981a, b).
sections.body: (pp. 5-73 to 5-74) Micropiles have been used for seismic retrofits where existing deep foundations lack capacity for the design earthquake; as discussed in Chapter 3, retrofits typically add micropiles to an existing foundation for overturning, uplift and lateral forces. Current guidance for seismic design of bridge foundations is Division I-A of AASHTO (2002), and these recommendations apply generally to micropiles under seismic effects; more is in JPWRI (2002). The seismic response of a pile foundation distributes superstructure loads into the soil through the piles (Figure 5-25), in general three translational forces (axial and two lateral shears) and three moments (torsion and two rotations about horizontal axes). Dynamic response can be evaluated by pseudo-static or dynamic response analysis; a realistic approach accounts for nonlinear near-surface soils and layering, so practice models the soil support by discrete nonlinear springs, the pile as a beam-column on lateral springs (p-y curves) and axial springs (t-z curves). Torsional resistance of individual piles is usually ignored for highway bridges, since group torsion resolves into lateral loads on individual piles. For vertical dynamic response, t-z curves are generally calculated over the whole pile length, by Lam and Martin (1986, 1997) and Kraft et al. (1981a, b).
key_points: Seismic retrofits add micropiles to existing foundations for overturning, uplift and lateral forces
Guidance: AASHTO (2002) Division I-A; JPWRI (2002)
Response involves three forces and three moments (Figure 5-25; Bryant and Matlock, 1977)
Pile modeled as a beam-column on nonlinear p-y (lateral) and t-z (axial) springs; torsion usually ignored for highway bridges
t-z curves over the whole length: Lam and Martin (1986, 1997), Kraft et al. (1981a, b)
