sections.title: Use of Battered Micropiles in Highly Seismic Regions
sections.summary: Vertical micropiles in groups do little against horizontal seismic deformation (FOREVER, 2003); battered micropiles have smaller positive but much higher negative head moments, and some U.S. owners disallow battered piles for seismic retrofit. Trinh et al. (2004) modeled twelve 178-mm (7-in.) micropiles battered 15 degrees inward and 25 degrees outward under a 4572 mm square, 915 mm high cap (Figure 5-26): with adequate cap flexural reinforcement, failure is micropile yielding or pullout, and a reinforcement ratio of about 0.5 percent gives fully ductile response (Figure 5-27).
sections.body: (pp. 5-75 to 5-76) Vertical micropiles in groups do little to resist horizontal seismic deformation because of their relatively low stiffness (FOREVER, 2003). Under seismic loading battered micropiles have a reduced positive bending moment compared with vertical micropiles but significantly higher negative bending moments at the pile head, and concern over excessive moments in the design event has led some U.S. owner agencies to disallow battered piles for seismic retrofit. Trinh et al. (2004) performed finite element analyses of combined axial compression and lateral displacement on battered micropiles: a square column on a 4572 mm by 4572 mm (180 in. by 180 in.), 915-mm (36-in.) high cap supported by twelve 178-mm (7-in.) micropiles (Figure 5-26), battered inward at 15 degrees and outward at 25 degrees from vertical. They concluded that with adequate flexural reinforcement in the cap the failure mode would mainly be yielding of the micropiles or pullout, with little if any yielding of the micropile-footing connection. Figure 5-27 shows the effect of cap reinforcement: a fully ductile response can be achieved with a flexural reinforcement ratio rho_s (flexural steel area over cross section area) of about 0.5 percent, ductility meaning no significant loss of lateral support at large displacements and/or a relatively large ratio of ultimate to yield deformation. If the connection were loaded more than expected it is expected to behave in a highly ductile manner, with failure by micropile pullout or yielding.
key_points: Vertical micropile groups do little against horizontal seismic deformation (FOREVER, 2003)
Battered micropiles: smaller positive but much higher negative head moments; some U.S. owners disallow them for seismic retrofit
Trinh et al. (2004): twelve 178 mm micropiles battered 15 deg inward and 25 deg outward under a 4572 mm square, 915 mm high cap (Figure 5-26)
With adequate cap flexural reinforcement, failure is micropile yielding or pullout, not the connection
Cap flexural reinforcement ratio of about 0.5 % gives a fully ductile response (Figure 5-27)

Figure 5-27: Lateral Response of Micropile Foundation for Different Flexural Reinforcement Ratio (after Trinh et al., 2004) (p. 5-76)

sections.title: Load Sharing with Existing Foundations
sections.summary: Seismic retrofit of an existing deep foundation requires evaluating load sharing; vertical micropiles are used for added compression and uplift (e.g., rocking). For old, deteriorated or poorly documented foundations, assume the micropiles alone carry the design seismic loads; consider sharing only with sufficient information (as-built drawings, load tests, calculations), using soil-structure interaction analyses.
sections.body: (pp. 5-76 to 5-77) Seismic retrofit of an existing deep foundation with micropiles requires evaluating load sharing between the existing elements and the micropiles; where added elements must support additional compression and uplift (e.g., rocking motions), vertical micropiles are used. For retrofit of an old or deteriorated foundation, or one whose original structural details and specifications are uncertain, design seismic loads should be assumed carried by the micropiles only. Load sharing between existing and new foundations should be considered only with sufficient information on the existing system (as-built drawings, load test results, design calculations), and then soil-structure interaction analyses are needed.
key_points: Retrofit requires evaluating load sharing between existing elements and micropiles; vertical micropiles for added compression and uplift (rocking)
Old, deteriorated or uncertain foundations: micropiles alone carry the design seismic loads
Consider load sharing only with as-built drawings, load tests or calculations, using soil-structure interaction analyses
sections.applicability: Load sharing between existing foundations and retrofit micropiles under seismic load.

sections.title: Pile Uplift Capacity
sections.summary: Seismic overturning puts large cyclic axial loads, including uplift, on the outer piles. AASHTO (2002) Division I-A 6.4.2(B) allows some separation of cap and soil (up to one-half the cap bearing area for groups) if the soil does not lose strength; 6.4.2(C) uses ultimate pile capacity for seismic uplift (FS = 1.0), with all other permanent loads included. Trinh et al. (2004) found large tension and severe cracking at outboard battered piles even under compression, so add vertical shear reinforcement near the outboard piles.
sections.body: (p. 5-77) Individual piles in groups are subjected to significant uplift under seismic loading: the overturning moment on the cap is resisted by axial pile resistance, the outermost piles taking relatively large cyclic axial loads. AASHTO (2002) Division I-A Section 6.4.2(B) suggests some separation between cap bottom and soil is allowed if the soil is not susceptible to loss of strength (e.g., liquefaction) under cyclic loading, up to one-half the cap bearing area for pile groups; Section 6.4.2(C) recommends using the ultimate pile capacity for seismic uplift (FS = 1.0 on geotechnical uplift capacity), with all other permanent loads included. Structural requirements, including pile embedment in the cap and connection detailing, also need consideration. In the Trinh et al. (2004) study, battered micropiles on the outboard side developed large tensile forces and relatively severe cracking even under large vertical compression; they concluded a prudent design increases vertical shear reinforcement (closer spacing) in the cap near the piles furthest from the column (the outboard piles) to mitigate cracking.
key_points: Seismic overturning gives large cyclic axial loads and uplift on the outer piles
AASHTO Division I-A 6.4.2(B): cap-soil separation allowed (up to one-half the bearing area for groups) if soil does not lose strength
AASHTO 6.4.2(C): ultimate capacity for seismic uplift (FS = 1.0), with all other permanent loads included
Consider pile embedment in the cap and connection detailing
Trinh et al. (2004): add vertical shear reinforcement in the cap near outboard piles to limit cracking
sections.applicability: Seismic uplift on micropile groups, AASHTO allowances and cap reinforcement near outboard piles.

sections.title: Liquefaction
sections.summary: Soil may not liquefy until the end of shaking, but because timing is uncertain, reduced vertical and lateral resistance is commonly assigned to potentially liquefiable soil. Lateral resistance in liquefied ground is about 0.1 to 1.0 percent of that in non-liquefied ground (Ishihara and Cubrinovski, 1998), so batter piles may be needed for lateral load after liquefaction, especially for flexible micropiles. FOREVER (2003): vertical micropiles did not reduce liquefaction; batter micropiles prevented it in their zone. Design batter pile caps for moments and the piles for lateral load from settlement.
sections.body: (pp. 5-77 to 5-79) In many earthquakes the soil may not liquefy until the end of shaking, so piles may still rely on support in the potentially liquefied zone during the earthquake; but because of uncertainty in timing, it is common to assign reduced vertical and lateral resistance to potentially liquefiable soil if the pile must carry load during and after the earthquake. Ishihara and Cubrinovski (1998) suggest the lateral resistance of a pile in liquefied ground is approximately 0.1 to 1.0 percent of that in non-liquefied ground, so if a foundation in potentially liquefiable soil must carry lateral loads after liquefaction, batter piles may be needed; this reduction is particularly important for relatively flexible micropiles. FOREVER (2003) studies showed vertical micropiles were not effective in reducing liquefaction, while batter micropiles limited seismically induced soil movement and pore pressure buildup, with no liquefaction in the zone affected by the piles while the free field liquefied. If batter piles are used, the cap connections should be designed for moments from lateral movements and the batter piles for lateral loads from soil settlement.
key_points: Liquefaction may come late in shaking, but timing is uncertain: assign reduced vertical and lateral resistance
Lateral resistance in liquefied ground about 0.1 to 1.0 % of non-liquefied (Ishihara and Cubrinovski, 1998)
Batter piles may be needed to carry lateral load after liquefaction, especially for flexible micropiles
FOREVER (2003): vertical micropiles did not reduce liquefaction; batter micropiles prevented it in their zone
With batter piles, design cap connections for moments and the piles for lateral loads from settlement
sections.applicability: Reduced support from liquefied soil and the role of batter micropiles.
